Making the World a Better Place

Notes on ideology, the Cold War, and the founding of the IAEA — read as a case study for AI governance
Contents

  2. Part Two — Building the IAEA: A Case Study in Governing Dangerous Technology
  3. Part Three — What AI Safety Might Take From This

Part One — Ideology and the Shape of the Cold War

Why look at the Cold War

Humans, and organizations more broadly, seem to fall into patterns of behavior. It is very hard to bring about scalable, consistent, positive change, and even when the pressure to change is high, it usually takes an entirely new team, a new culture, and a new way of thinking before anything actually shifts. While digging through AI safety work, I found that much of it was focused on policy, which is unsurprising and more or less what I expected. What surprised me more was how much ideology, and a particular way of life, ended up dictating that policy.

To get a grasp of the repeating patterns in organizations, and of the ideological differences between large nation-states, I decided to look at one period in particular: the early 1940s through the late 1970s, an era shaped heavily by the Cold War. It was not a traditional war, even though bloodshed and human-rights violations were plentiful on every side — it was a war of ideology, of ways of life, and of fear of the unknown. I was surprised by how much the events of the time were shaped by ideology. As something of an outsider to all of it, I was taken aback by how much influence a nation-state can have over the lives of its people, and by how new ideologies — sometimes on the extreme ends of the spectrum — kept emerging even inside heavily constructed regimes.

The obvious winner to emerge from this period is the United States, along with its principles of the free market and democracy, and its broader ideals of liberty and the American way of life. To understand what eventually led to the Soviet collapse, it helps to first understand why such a flawed system as communism managed to take root in the first place. The Soviet Union had long endured severe regimes under the Tsars and had witnessed, firsthand, the brutality of autocratic rule — class inequality, centuries of oppression, and soldiers pressed unwillingly into the expansion of the Russian empire. What tends to follow a long and tedious regime is simply an overcorrection, and much of the ideology that followed was built on standards that were idealistic rather than grounded in reason.

The break with Germany, and the roots of mutual distrust

One of the biggest blows to the Soviet Union's moral standing in the eyes of the rest of the world was Stalin's initial stance toward the Nazi regime. Russia's position had been uneven even during the volatile years of the First World War, from which it eventually withdrew partway through. Despite later losing enormous numbers of people trying to hold back Nazi Germany, the Soviet Union's initial stance was far more moderate, and it was even allied with the Nazi regime at the outset. It was only once Hitler's forces reached Russian soil that the Soviets recognized their mistake and fell back.

So why did two regimes that had fought side by side end up as such bitterly separate enemies? Much of it has to do with Soviet espionage, and with the United States' refusal to share its nuclear plans with what it saw as an unstable regime — a decision that arguably triggered a long and gruelling arms race, a funny sort of contest for the bigger stick that neither side could actually use. What followed was a much harsher framing for the rest of the world: either you were with one side, or you were against it.

One of the reasons that framing was possible at all has to do with the sheer scale of human degradation the world had just witnessed under the Nazi regime. Around the same time, much of the colonized world was fighting its own moral war for independence, while often committing comparable atrocities of its own. That did not sit well with the former colonial powers, especially once they found themselves fighting alongside the United States — itself a former colony, and an outspoken advocate for democratic values. As the concepts of nationalism and of a distinct local identity began to take hold in the colonies, people were left with little real choice but to fight or die. And with the advent of the printing press and a freer global media, the atrocities on every side could no longer be hidden from the rest of the world — the hypocrisy of claiming to fight a moral war while behaving otherwise became impossible to sustain. The persecution of well-known researchers who had worked for the old colonial powers also left a deep and lasting distrust in the newly independent colonies.

Decolonization and the ideological vacuum

When the former colonizers, Britain chief among them, finally left, they left behind an ideological vacuum. Policies of divide-and-rule had deeply destabilized many of the local regimes they departed from. Much of the Eastern Bloc, Southeast Asia, and the Indian and African subcontinents were experiencing independence for the first time, and each had to choose an ideology that actually worked for them. A deep distrust of the former colonizers effectively narrowed the choice down to two live options: American-style values, or communism.

The United States genuinely believed that communism behaved like an ideological virus — that once a country was "infected," a domino effect would follow. At the time, the Soviet Union was essentially the only place where communism had been tried at scale, and its longer-term effects were still poorly understood. Much of the free press was still controlled by a small number of organizations, and because English was the primary language of that press, a great many opinions and voices from the newly independent colonies were left out of the conversation entirely. The former colonizers' attempts to justify their own historical conduct did little to win over the wider public. One of the biggest blows to the United States' own standing in the new world, in fact, was its close association with its wartime allies, who were also the old colonial powers. The next phase of the Cold War would be shaped heavily by that association.

The Space Race and its domestic consequences

By the early 1950s, the battleground had shifted to something very different: the kind of progress humanity, as a whole, should be striving for. With pressure mounting on both sides, and the world's emerging economies watching closely, the two superpowers eventually looked up — to the sky, the one battleground still open for a contest of pure innovation. This was one of the genuinely useful byproducts of the Cold War: the Space Race reshaped the education systems of both countries. Subjects like mathematics and the sciences, and some of the top engineering academies, were funded as a direct consequence. By the time the 1950s were drawing to a close, the scaffolding was in place, and Russia took the early lead, launching Sputnik, the first satellite — something now quietly watching from orbit, able to pass over facilities and locations below. It scared a great deal of the United States. The American government responded by funding its own research labs like never before, and by the late 1960s it had put a man on the Moon.

Programs like the Peace Corps, under the Kennedy administration, advocated for social reform in the newly emerging world and helped cement the push for American diplomacy and the broader ideals of American capitalism abroad.

One of the direct consequences of this renewed investment in science was a wave of knock-on innovation: the interstate highway system, and much of the groundwork for modern computing. An emphasis on science, among a younger generation that had grown up watching science fiction, combined with a society that rewarded innovation, progress, and genuine meritocracy, and modern America as we now know it began to take shape. Alongside this, rapid industrialization pushed people out of the cities and into the suburbs, where they hoped to raise a family and buy a house. The modern suburban structure, and the neighborhood as a distinct social unit — something that does not really exist in quite the same form elsewhere in the world — emerged from this period, with people of similar social standing clustering together. The culture of building a company out of your own garage and scaling it to reach millions of people, and the rise of chains — restaurants, supermarkets, and a broader culture of brand loyalty — all took hold at scale for the first time. Modern capitalism, in its fullest form, was born.

The Red Scare and McCarthyism

It was a turbulent time. Red Scare advocates like Senator McCarthy largely succumbed to their own misfortune; the negativity his radical campaigns spread eventually turned him into a demagogue in the eyes of history. Even after McCarthy's own death from alcoholism, many of the institutions he had championed continued to operate well into the late 1970s.

The Civil Rights Movement

One of the defining issues of this period was the civil rights movement. Many of the soldiers who had fought in the Second World War came from African American communities, and once they returned home, the injustice of segregation — despite deep resistance from the American South — became something the government could no longer ignore. A new generation of intellectuals from within these communities became radicalized, and a wave of marches and demonstrations eventually forced the government toward real, if overdue, policy change.

Part Two — Building the IAEA: A Case Study in Governing Dangerous Technology

I came across a particularly interesting book on the establishment of the IAEA and the broader project of nuclear non-proliferation. Going in, I was fairly skeptical, with a somewhat prejudiced and heavily biased opinion of older institutions and their procedures. I was wrong. For better or worse, what actually slowed the nuclear race down was each side simply having the bigger stick in hand — a strange enough phenomenon in the world of policy and diplomacy on its own. The history of nuclear development, from its inception to its eventual slowdown, has been painful, stressful, and often riddled with outsized egos, bureaucratic arm-twisting, and a great deal of plain politics. We were lucky, in a sense, that it took something so sinister, and powerful enough to cause destruction on a scale that is not just an existential risk but something closer to an s-risk, to force that slowdown at all.

To better understand the human psyche, and the moral and psychological compass of people living in very different parts of the world, I tried to take the lessons of these earlier institutions and bring them into the present. This section is heavily inspired by a short, nine-page document from Safer AI.

Before the bomb

The science that made all of this possible goes back to the 1920s and 30s, and to work by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann, who bombarded uranium with neutrons and, in doing so, split the atom — discovering nuclear fission almost by accident. What made the discovery so consequential was the realization that a fission reaction could, under the right conditions, become self-sustaining: each split atom releases more neutrons, which go on to split further atoms, releasing yet more neutrons in turn, in a chain reaction. The potential applications of that insight, for power and for weapons alike, were worked out and debated by physicists almost immediately.

It was against that backdrop that Albert Einstein wrote his now-famous letter to President Roosevelt, warning that Nazi Germany might be pursuing a bomb of its own and urging the United States to act first. That letter, more than anything else, led to the creation and commissioning of the Manhattan Project. Los Alamos, New Mexico, was chosen as its central laboratory — remote, defensible, and far from prying eyes — and it was there that J. Robert Oppenheimer assembled the team that would go on to build the bomb.

The implosion design eventually used at Los Alamos: a spherical shockwave from conventional explosives compressing a plutonium core past criticality.

Plutonium itself was discovered only shortly before the project began, and Enrico Fermi's criticality experiments — assembling just enough fissile material to sustain, and then halt, a chain reaction — were essential to proving the theory could work in practice. Those working closest to the material spoke of a strange, pale blue glow that would appear around a critical mass in the dark: Cherenkov radiation, the visible signature of particles moving faster than light can travel through water or air. It became something of a quiet, unsettling omen among the physicists who worked with it — beautiful and lethal in more or less equal measure.

Niels Bohr sent his own memorandum to the American president, warning of the political consequences of the bomb and urging early international control before a race could begin in earnest. Much of the Manhattan Project's scientific core, meanwhile, was made up of physicists who had fled Nazi Germany — Bohr among them, alongside others who brought with them both expertise the Allies badly needed and firsthand knowledge of exactly what Germany's own bomb program might be capable of. Their presence was arguably as important politically as it was scientifically: it was proof, to the Americans, that the German threat was real.

From Trinity to the stockpile race

The Trinity test, in the New Mexico desert, was the moment the theory finally became a weapon. Oppenheimer and Truman met with the other Allied powers shortly afterward, at Potsdam, where Truman mentioned to Stalin, almost in passing, that the United States now possessed a new weapon of unusual destructive force. Stalin's famously muted reaction at the time masked how shaken the Soviet leadership actually was — Soviet intelligence had already told them roughly what was coming. The bomb itself yielded in the range of twenty kilotons, a figure that would look almost modest next to what followed within the next decade.

The detonations over Hiroshima and Nagasaki settled, for the moment, the question of whether the weapon worked. What they did not settle was the much harder question of what to do next: whether, and how, to share the underlying science with other nations, including wartime allies. Soviet distrust deepened sharply once the bomb had actually been used, and a secret race to build the larger stockpile was effectively already underway.

The first real attempt at an answer came in 1946, when Bernard Baruch presented a plan to the United Nations for what would have been the first international atomic development authority — a body with the power to gather information on nuclear programs worldwide, and to apply sanctions or punishment where violations were found. The Soviet Union rejected it, largely over the veto power the plan would have left in the hands of the UN Security Council's permanent members, the US included. In the absence of any agreed international control, Washington instead pushed to restrict commerce in nuclear material between states, citing the genuine rarity of natural fissile ore, while European powers scrambled to secure their own sources of uranium ore, much of it out of the Belgian Congo.

The American monopoly did not last. The Soviet Union conducted its first nuclear test in August 1949, cutting short Western intelligence estimates that had given it another two decades. Britain followed with its own test in October 1952. By 1953, Eisenhower had succeeded Truman in the White House, and in April of 1952 — just before the handover — a Panel of Consultants on Disarmament had already been formed, which fed into what became known as the "Candor" effort: an attempt to level with the American public about just how dangerous the new nuclear landscape actually was.

Then came the hydrogen bomb. The first American test, in November 1952, was followed by a Soviet equivalent within less than a year, and real panic set in on both sides. The same disarmament panel began pressing, for the first time, for real and enforceable controls over fissile material itself, rather than simply counting finished warheads. Public anxiety over fallout grew alongside the stockpiles — strontium-90 turning up in milk and other everyday foods became one of the more visceral symbols of what atmospheric testing actually meant for ordinary people.

What the testing program was, in the end, rehearsing for.

That pressure turned to alarm on the first of March, 1954, when the Castle Bravo test at Bikini Atoll produced a yield far larger than its designers had predicted, and the fallout drifted over Rongelap Atoll and over a Japanese fishing boat, the Daigo Fukuryū Maru — the "Lucky Dragon" — contaminating its crew. It remains one of the starkest cautionary tales to come out of the entire testing era, and it is what finally turned "suspend all nuclear testing" from a fringe position into a serious international demand.

Eisenhower's "Atoms for Peace," and the case for an international agency

Eisenhower's own answer to the moment was his "Atoms for Peace" proposal, delivered to the United Nations in December 1953 — bleak in parts, but an attempt to offer a way out of the spiral: redirect fissile material away from weapons and toward peaceful uses, under the watch of a new international body. Public perception of nuclear technology at the time swung between genuine awe and genuine dread — an "atomic colossus," as some called it then, promising limitless power with one hand while holding civilizational destruction in the other. The idea of pooling fissile material into shared international "banks," available for peaceful research and power generation, was central to the plan, and it is hard not to notice the parallel with the way large AI labs today talk about compute and model weights — a resource valuable enough, and dangerous enough, that someone has to decide who gets access to it and on what terms.

The proposal was met with real skepticism on both sides. Supporters saw a genuine, if imperfect, path to defusing the arms race and spreading the civilian benefits of nuclear power through real cooperation and a shared belief in the greater good — however unevenly that belief was actually held. Critics worried it would simply spread nuclear know-how and material more widely, making proliferation easier rather than harder, while doing little to actually slow weapons production where it already existed. Both readings had a case, and both would turn out to be at least partly right.

The IAEA takes shape

By 1957, the International Atomic Energy Agency existed on paper. What it looked like in practice took years to work out. Despite resistance from the Soviet Union and India, the Agency's Western-aligned Board members pushed through the first safeguards system on a small scale in 1959, applied initially to just three tons of natural uranium that Canada had supplied to Japan. In 1961, the Board approved its first proper safeguards system, covering research reactors up to 100 megawatts thermal. Standing committees on budget, programme, and technical assistance were set up that same founding year, and — tellingly — no new ones have been created since. Member states, and especially the major powers, have continued to shape IAEA policy through the Board, the General Conference, and direct bilateral contact ever since; somewhat ironically, the area where they have pressed the Director General hardest and most persistently is staff appointments, even though the Agency's own Statute makes personnel decisions the Director General's exclusive preserve.

The fight over who would actually run the Agency was its own small drama. The early frontrunner, Sterling Cole, lacked support from the Kennedy administration and was unpopular with Western Europeans. A widely respected alternative, Paul Jolles, could have been a non-contentious successor, but had already taken a senior post in the Swiss government by the time the question came up. The United States instead pushed for a neutral scientist, Sigvard Eklund, well regarded across the European nuclear establishment. The Soviet Union, having already accepted an American in the role back in 1957, wanted a Director General of its own from the socialist bloc, and first proposed a three-way "troika" arrangement under a Bulgarian candidate. When that failed, Moscow threw its support behind the Indonesian ambassador instead, backed by African and Asian states. The General Conference confirmed Eklund by a vote of 46 to 16, with five abstentions. The Soviet delegate, Emelyanov, walked out of the vote, announced he would have no contact with the new Director General, and reportedly refused to speak with him or answer his letters for some time afterward. Soviet officials went as far as describing IAEA safeguards as a "spider's web," designed by capitalist powers to strangle the nuclear progress of developing countries.

That hostility did not last. Eklund was reappointed with full Soviet support in 1965, 1969, 1973, and 1977, and the Soviets may well have backed him again in 1981 had he not chosen to retire and become Director General Emeritus instead. Between 1961 and 1981, the Agency's main programmes reached maturity, nuclear power orders in the West rose and then leveled off, and non-proliferation became firmly established as one of the Agency's central functions. Technical assistance to developing countries grew from roughly $2.3 million in 1961 to roughly $24.4 million by 1981.

For most of those two decades, Washington and Moscow effectively ran the IAEA in concert. Fears of proliferation grew sharply through the 1960s — the Cuban Missile Crisis, the arrival of new nuclear states, NATO's own proposals, and persistent rumors about German, Italian, and Israeli ambitions all played a part. Kennedy himself warned that the world could see somewhere between fifteen and twenty-five nuclear-armed states by the mid-1970s if nothing changed, which only hardened the resolve, on both sides, to contain proliferation through IAEA safeguards. The 1970s, in turn, brought a genuine surge in nuclear power orders — first in North America, then in Europe, and then, tentatively, in parts of the developing world.

Away from the politics, the Agency also built a real scientific legacy. In 1964, the Board accepted Eklund's proposal for a theoretical physics centre in Trieste, alongside a joint division with the FAO on nuclear techniques in food and agriculture. Other early landmarks included an expanded marine radioactivity laboratory in Monaco and the Agency's own laboratories at Seibersdorf, outside Vienna. Eklund himself tended to leave the biggest political storms to be settled directly between Washington and Moscow — a pattern some came to call a "superpower condominium" over the Agency in the later 1960s — while quietly eliminating wasteful practices, cutting unnecessary reports, reducing travel, and streamlining the Board's own procedures. By 1962–63, Board debates had become noticeably less confrontational, helped along by a shift in who was actually sitting at the table: national nuclear energy officials increasingly replaced career diplomats as the majority of Governors. Eklund made a habit of consulting national missions before Board meetings to secure compromises in private and avoid contested votes wherever possible, and by 1974 the General Conference had abolished one of its two main committees entirely, compressing its remaining work into a single week.

Something softer than any formal procedure also seemed to take hold during these years — people at the time referred to it as the "spirit of Vienna." Living and working together in a single city over long stretches of time appears to have instilled a deeper mutual respect among the delegates and the secretariat than any committee structure could have produced on its own. With the Agency's infrastructure still genuinely new, most countries simply sent their own working scientists as representatives rather than professional diplomats, which, in itself, built a surprising amount of solidarity: heads of national nuclear authorities understood one another first as fellow scientists facing broadly similar problems, and only second as representatives of competing states. The Austrian government and the city of Vienna contributed their own share of goodwill and, as the saying went, Gemütlichkeit. It is tempting to wonder whether a similarly concentrated hub produces some of the same effect today — the Bay Area is the closest rough analogue, with a large share of the world's AI safety labs clustered within roughly thirty miles of one another. In 1965, the General Conference was held outside Vienna for the first time, in Tokyo, marking both Japan's growing stature and the twentieth anniversary of Hiroshima; holding the meeting somewhere the consequences of the technology could be witnessed firsthand seems to have mattered to the delegates in ways a Vienna meeting never could.

Representation on the Board was its own long-running fight. By 1960, African and Middle Eastern membership had grown substantially, but the original 1957 Statute allotted the entire region just one elective Board seat. South Africa proposed adding two more seats for the region, and in 1961 both the Board and the General Conference approved the change, while also confirming that Latin America would hold three elective seats of its own. The General Conference asked the Board to formally review the relevant article of the Statute in 1968, and a committee was duly set up the following year. With the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty about to enter into force, West Germany and Italy grew anxious that they would soon be pressured into placing their own nuclear industries under IAEA safeguards, and argued this justified permanent Board seats of their own — seats that Japan and Canada had, in effect, already held since the Agency's Preparatory Commission. The Italian ambassador, Roberto Ducci, led the push to expand the Board's top category from five seats to nine, creating room for two more permanent Western European members. The amendment that eventually passed increased the top category to nine seats, reduced the number of regional leader seats from five to three, and raised the number of elective seats from twelve to twenty-two, for a new Board total of thirty-four. The Middle East was detached from Africa and attached instead to South Asia, creating two new regional categories — "Africa," and "the Middle East and South Asia" — and in 1970, after considerable debate, the General Conference approved the substance of the Italian proposal by majority vote, over the objections of the Soviet Union, its allies, and South Africa. Once the Middle East had been separated from Africa, another African state could take the seat South Africa had held; in 1977, the Board designated Egypt to fill it.

Deciding exactly which country counted as the "most advanced" nuclear nation within a given region, for the purposes of a Board seat, was rarely straightforward. Much of Western Europe's seat tended to rotate among Switzerland, Sweden, Belgium, and Italy — nations that, between them, held a disproportionate share of the era's most capable nuclear engineers — but the competition for regional recognition could get genuinely heated. When Argentina challenged Brazil's own designation in 1962, an independent panel of experts concluded there simply wasn't enough evidence to say definitively that either country was more advanced than the other. Similar rivalries played out between South Africa and Egypt in the African region, and among several states across Latin America.

China's seat was a recurring flashpoint at every single General Conference. The Soviet Union, its allies, and a growing number of non-aligned countries repeatedly pushed to reject the credentials of "Nationalist" China and seat the People's Republic instead, and the issue only grew more divisive as more Western countries, alongside the entire socialist bloc, extended the People's Republic formal recognition. Moscow pushed, in parallel, for the admission of the German Democratic Republic, the then People's Republic of Vietnam, and several other states not yet seated at the table.

By 1979, the Agency finally moved out of Vienna's Grand Hotel — its "temporary" home for roughly twenty years — into the purpose-built Vienna International Centre, on a peppercorn rent of one Austrian schilling a year.

Verification, privatization, and the bomb nobody could hide

The IAEA's role in verifying a test ban turned out to be more limited than its early advocates expected. In July 1958, the Soviet Union and the West began drafting a treaty to ban all nuclear testing, and from July through August of that year, experts from eight nations met in Geneva to study how underground tests might actually be detected. They proposed a mix of land- and ship-based monitoring stations, weather-reconnaissance aircraft, and some kind of international control body to oversee it all. The IAEA looked, on paper, like the obvious candidate — it was already the only global atomic authority with its own inspection principles and safeguards personnel in place. The United States declared an unlimited moratorium on nuclear testing on the 31st of October, 1958; the Soviet Union had already done the same back in March. But the West never quite treated test-ban verification as a "peaceful" activity in the way the IAEA's founding mandate was meant to cover, and when negotiators finally drafted the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty in 1996, they chose not to give the IAEA the verification role after all, for reasons that were never especially well articulated. The CTBT does still require close cooperation between its own organization, the CTBTO, and the IAEA, which leaves at least some room for a working relationship between the two.

The peacetime half of the bargain: nuclear power moving, gradually, out of government hands.

Nuclear energy itself was also moving, in parallel, toward private ownership. The Atomic Energy Act of 1959, in the United States, opened the door to private industry owning and operating nuclear material and reactors directly, rather than leaving the entire field in government hands — its own small, early echo of the tension in AI today between state-funded research and the growing share of frontier capability sitting inside private labs.

The stockpile the whole agency was, in the end, built to try to contain.

And looming over all of it, as a kind of closing marker for the sheer scale the stockpile race had reached, was the Tsar Bomba — a fifty-megaton Soviet device, detonated on the 30th of October, 1961, that remains the single largest explosion ever caused by human beings. It was built by a team that included Andrei Sakharov, among others, and its sheer size appears to have unsettled even the people who built it.

Part Three — What AI Safety Might Take From This

The scale of failure a future governing body would exist to prevent.

We may be at a point where AI is capable of causing serious damage but still lacks the autonomy to pursue goals that could be genuinely harmful to humanity on its own. That phase has a real historical precedent: the long-term effects of radioactive fallout were not well understood either, in the early stages of the race to acquire more of it, and much of the world simply gave up on guardrails while that uncertainty lasted. Geoffrey Hinton has made a related point in his own way — that the world may need some number of smaller-scale AI failures or shutdowns before it takes the actual consequences of the technology seriously, in something like the way Castle Bravo and the Lucky Dragon finally made nuclear fallout real to people who had only read about it before.

The rest of this section is less a finished argument and more a working list of the questions the IAEA's history raised for me, organized roughly by theme. I don't think all of them have clean answers yet — some of them may not have clean answers at all — but they feel like the right questions to be asking.

Material and compute governance

  • What would a genuine parallel to the IAEA's fissile-material banks look like for AI model weights, or for the compute used to train frontier models?
  • Do export and enrichment controls on uranium offer any real template for export controls on advanced chips, or for rules around fine-tuning and activation-based interventions on existing models?
  • What would a clear, trustworthy audit trail for chip production actually require — tracking how many chips are made, who is involved at each stage, where the real bottlenecks in the supply chain sit, and what happens when a shipment fails or is diverted?
  • Nuclear technology, for most of this history, stayed in state hands. A meaningful share of frontier AI capability today sits inside private companies instead — what does that change about who a future governing body would actually need jurisdiction over?

Verification, safeguards, and detection

  • What can the long, difficult history of nuclear test-ban verification teach a field that is just beginning to think about verifying claims made about model training runs?
  • What would meaningful guardrails on data centers actually look like — a genuinely unified, trust-based network for sharing information across organizations that otherwise compete with one another?
  • How would a monitoring body detect real signs of misalignment, or anything resembling consciousness, inside systems whose internals most outside observers cannot directly inspect?
  • What would a verification mechanism that cannot be quietly tampered with by the organization being verified actually look like in practice?
  • Is there a version of this where a unified body monitors large training runs across every major data center in the world, the way the IAEA eventually monitored fissile material?

Representation and institutional power

  • The IAEA's Board seats were, in the end, mostly a story about which states could develop and control nuclear material — a short list, because the capability itself was concentrated in a short list of states. AI is different: nearly every developed and developing nation will be affected by it, which makes an equal say for all of them feel important in a way it never quite was for nuclear weapons, where only governments could really build them. For AI, capability is already far more dispersed.
  • If a nation feels pressured by the threat of tighter global regulation, the IAEA's history suggests it will usually respond by pushing for more seats at the table to leverage decisions in its own favor, rather than by simply accepting the pressure. Should we expect the same pattern here?
  • Is there a meaningful difference between a seat that lets a state verify what others are doing, and a seat that actually lets it shape how the technology gets developed? The IAEA's own history suggests states developing a given technology often prefer governing bodies with only the former power, not the latter.
  • What does a modern equivalent of regional bloc politics — the old fights over "most advanced nation" status, or over which bloc a given country belongs to — look like for AI, where the geography of capability doesn't map cleanly onto the old nuclear map at all?

Leadership and process

  • How should a Director-General equivalent for an AI safety body actually be chosen, and by whom?
  • What should its standing committees look like — budget, programme, technical assistance — and should the same restraint the IAEA showed, no new standing committees since 1959, apply here too?
  • How do you keep an organization's permanent members and its major funders from simply running the organization by mutual agreement, the way Washington and Moscow effectively ran the IAEA for two decades?
  • How should disagreements actually get resolved — through private consultation before a vote, the way Eklund tended to operate, or in the open?
  • What belongs in the public eye, and what doesn't?

Talent, movement, and containment

  • How do you protect the free movement of AI safety researchers when individual nations can unilaterally restrict travel or export for their own reasons?
  • Expert opinion on what counts as safe, or acceptable, varies enormously across cultures and institutions — whose moral standards should actually count as representative of humanity as a whole when a model is being trained or evaluated?
  • If a genuinely capable system is built and the decision is made to keep running it rather than shut it down, where should the containment facility actually sit, and who gets to decide?
  • Would such a system need its own sandboxed version of the internet to operate inside, and what are the ethical consequences of keeping something like that contained indefinitely?

Escalation and deterrence

  • If a state wanted to turn a powerful model's capabilities against an adversary, what would de-escalation actually look like, and what communication channels would need to exist before that happens, rather than after?

The role of international bodies

  • Does the world need something like a second IAEA, built specifically for AI safety, and what role could an existing body like the United Nations realistically play in shaping that kind of policy?

Threads for the next draft

A few topics I still want to come back to, that this draft doesn't really get into yet: Nixon's visits to China and the Soviet Union, and what they changed; the fall of the Eastern Bloc; a closer look at the Red Scare beyond McCarthy himself; the Space Race as a direct investment parallel to today's AI research spending; the idea of a "bubble" of progress, and what an intelligence explosion might actually look like in practice; a fuller treatment of nuclear disarmament as a parallel to AI disarmament, if that's even the right word for it; how AI safety is being approached outside the US and China; and, more broadly, what ideologies and what laws end up governing an age shaped by AI, the way the Cold War's ideologies ended up governing the back half of the twentieth century.
